conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were transferred here from the other hospital because of fever and nausea. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve had a fever off and on for a few days, up to 101.6, and I’ve been feeling really nauseous. Not much pain, though—my usual pancreatitis pain is worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And any vomiting, chills, or changes in how you’re eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. But I’ve had chills—shaking, teeth chattering. And I haven’t been eating much. My urine’s been dark, so I know I’m not drinking enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ve reviewed your records. You have chronic pancreatitis and use a Hickman line for TPN at home. Your labs from the other hospital showed a high creatinine—3.6—suggesting your kidneys were stressed, likely from dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. But I’ve been on a diet for two weeks now. This came out of nowhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re concerned. This doesn’t look like a typical flare. We’ve started you on IV fluids to help your kidneys and keep you hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. But why the fever? Is it an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking for that. Blood cultures were sent at the other hospital and again here. We’ll know more in a day or two. For now, we’re keeping you on your regular pain and nausea meds and watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my TPN? Should I restart that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV fluids and nutrients for now. We’ll decide about TPN once we know more about the infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your first blood cultures didn’t grow anything, but we’re still waiting on others. Your creatinine dropped to 2.7, so your kidneys are improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I still feel shaky and tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring you closely. We did a chest X-ray yesterday—no pneumonia. EKG was normal too. We’re watching for any sign of infection spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about my Hickman line? It’s been fine for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a possibility. Lines like that can sometimes become a source of infection, even without obvious signs. We’ll know more when the next cultures come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have news. One of your blood cultures grew a yeast called Candida parapsilosis. It’s likely coming from your Hickman line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeast? In my blood? That sounds serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but you’re not showing severe symptoms, which is a good sign. We’re starting you on an IV antifungal called micafungin to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay in the hospital for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. We also need to remove the Hickman line because it’s the most likely source. We’ll schedule that for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about my TPN? I need that at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold TPN for now. After the line is out and we finish treatment, you can get a new one placed if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will this yeast affect my heart or eyes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. We’ve arranged an echocardiogram and an eye exam to check for that. Both are precautionary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your echo and eye exam came back normal—no signs of infection there. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to remove your Hickman line this morning. The tip will be sent to the lab to confirm the infection source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get local anesthesia. It might feel like pressure, but not sharp pain. The team will take good care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The line was successfully removed. The tip was sent for culture. You did great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m glad that’s over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest blood cultures are negative—no more yeast growing. That means the treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. We’ll switch you from IV micafungin to oral fluconazole—400 mg daily—for 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s usually well-tolerated. But it can increase the effect of your fentanyl patch. If you feel overly sleepy or dizzy, you might consider using only one patch instead of two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll pay attention to that. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your primary doctor in two days. They’ll draw blood cultures to make sure the infection is gone. Your pancreatologist will also see you soon for your chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when can I get a new TPN line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two weeks after finishing fluconazole, we’ll repeat blood cultures. If they’re negative, you can get a new line placed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve done well. All your repeat blood cultures are negative. We’re ready to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. What meds should I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual medications. Take fluconazole 400 mg daily for 14 days. Use Tums as needed for heartburn, and your nausea meds if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my fentanyl patches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now on one 100 mcg/hr patch every 72 hours. Monitor for drowsiness, especially with the fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And if I feel feverish again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor right away. Otherwise, keep your follow-up appointments and finish all the fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my diarrhea. It’s better now, but what caused it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool and ruled out C. diff. It was likely related to the infection or antibiotics. It should resolve on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re all set to go home. The nurse will give you discharge papers and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll follow up as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Stay hydrated, rest, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.
